overview: CDI is a nationwide New Zealand land developer with more than 30 years of experience acquiring raw/greenfield land, obtaining planning consents, and subdividing it into residential (and some commercial/industrial) sections for sale to builders and homeowners, primarily in Auckland, Hamilton, Havelock North (Hawke's Bay) and Christchurch (Canterbury). Since 2019 it has deliberately layered on a smaller, recurring-income commercial/industrial property rental portfolio (warehousing at Wiri, Auckland, and retail centres in Christchurch/Rolleston) to cushion the cyclicality of section sales. CDI is majority owned (65.12%) by NZX-listed Millennium & Copthorne Hotels New Zealand Limited (MCK), itself controlled by the Hong Leong/City Developments Limited (CDL) group of Singapore, giving CDI a well-capitalised, patient corporate parent and a historically debt-free balance sheet.

business_model.summary: CDI's core engine is the land-bank cycle: acquire raw or lightly-zoned land (often at a discount reflecting pre-consent risk), fund multi-year planning/consenting and civil-works (earthworks, roading, water/wastewater infrastructure), then sell titled sections to builders, developers and owner-occupiers. Revenue is recognised only on full settlement (transfer of Certificate of Title), so it is lumpy, project- and settlement-timed rather than a steady run-rate, and can swing materially between periods depending on which stages settle. Historically nearly all land is held at the lower of cost and net realisable value (not fair-valued), so the balance sheet materially understates the land bank's market value relative to independent valuations (FY2025: residential portfolio carried value implicit within $257.9m non-current + $17.6m current development property vs $339.3m independent market valuation). Since 2019 CDI has retained selected commercial/industrial lots post-subdivision (Wiri warehousing, Prestons Park and Stonebrook retail centres) to earn recurring rental income, diversifying earnings through the residential cycle. The land-development side is working-capital intensive: FY2025 operating cash flow was an $9.0m outflow because $24.0m of net investment went into growing development property (land purchases $14.8m + development spend $26.4m) even though profit after tax was $11.1m positive.

revenue_streams.name: Residential/property sales
revenue_streams.trend: declining (softer market, 87 sections sold FY2025 vs 92 FY2024, $34.5m vs $46.0m)

revenue_streams.name: Rental income (investment property)
revenue_streams.trend: growing (up ~20% YoY as portfolio matures; $2.3m warehouses + $0.9-1.2m retail; c.90-100% occupancy on warehouses, 83% on retail)

business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2B (building companies, developers who buy sections in bulk) with some direct-to-owner-occupier sales; commercial/industrial tenants for the rental leg (warehousing and suburban retail)
business_model.geographic_mix: Landholdings ~305 hectares nationwide: Hamilton/Waikato ~46% (140.6ha, largely the Ruakura 2 growth cell), Hawke's Bay ~26% (79.7ha, Iona/Arataki, Havelock North), Auckland ~14% (43.3ha, Trig Road/West Harbour), Canterbury ~5% (Prestons Park, Wairakei Road, Worsleys Road, Christchurch), Nelson/Tasman ~9% (Lucas Terrace, Highland Drive, Pelorus Sound). All revenue and assets are New Zealand-only (no offshore operations).

main_competitors: Kāinga Ora (state housing/urban development, land supply competitor and customer)
Regional/private developers (e.g., Universal Homes, Ryman-adjacent land holders)
Local councils and Crown entities as alternative land suppliers via Fast-track/urban growth programmes
competitive_position.market_position: A mid-sized, nationally-diversified niche player rather than the largest developer; scale is modest relative to Fletcher Building but CDI's balance-sheet strength, zero legacy debt and patient Singapore-linked ownership let it hold land through down-cycles that force smaller/leveraged private developers to sell distressed inventory or halt projects.

moat_factors.description: $Nil debt (until the Aug-2026 ANZ facility) and $13.4m cash at 31-Dec-2025 let CDI hold land through downturns without forced sales, unlike leveraged developers; this is the single biggest structural advantage in a cyclical, capital-intensive industry.

Development property is carried at lower of cost and net realisable value; independent valuers put residential portfolio market value at $339.3m vs a materially lower carrying cost, implying substantial unrecognised embedded margin on legacy land parcels (e.g., Prestons Park land bought 2004-2018).

moat_factors.factor: Parent backing (MCK / Hong Leong / CDL Singapore)
moat_factors.description: 65.12% owner MCK is in turn 83.84%-owned by CDL Hotels Holdings NZ, a subsidiary of London-listed Millennium & Copthorne Hotels Ltd, ultimately controlled by Hong Leong Investment Holdings Pte Ltd (Singapore). This gives CDI access to a globally significant, well-capitalised property group's expertise and capital discipline, and effectively insulates it from a hostile takeover, but concentrates strategic control.
Ten development sites spread across five regions and a growing rental leg (9.4% of FY2025 revenue) reduce single-market and pure-cyclicality risk versus a single-region pure-play subdivider.

Early, proactive use of the 2024 Fast-track Approvals Act (Arataki Road approved Feb-2026, Ruakura 2 and other applications to be lodged 2026) can compress multi-year RMA consenting timelines by roughly two years per management, a repeatable advantage for a developer with in-house planning capability and existing landholdings versus market entrants.

weaknesses: No scale/cost advantage versus Fletcher Building or larger integrated developers; limited negotiating leverage with contractors in a tight construction labour market
Small, highly concentrated executive team (CEO institutional knowledge risk explicitly flagged by the Board) versus larger peers' bench strength
Rental portfolio is tiny in absolute terms ($68.9m valuation, 4 properties) — not yet large enough to fully offset a prolonged residential downturn
Reliant on discretionary, interest-rate-and-confidence-sensitive residential buyers with no recurring subscription-like revenue outside the small rental book

growth_drivers: Fast-track Approvals Act pipeline: Arataki Road (171 residential sections, Havelock North) received Fast-track consent Feb-2026, ~2 years faster than conventional RMA process, with first sections expected late 2027; Ruakura 2 Growth Cell (140.6ha, Hamilton, circa 1,350 residential lots plus 35ha of commercial/industrial land) targeted for Fast-track lodgement by end-2026; a further Fast-track application in Havelock North (Iona Stage 3 / Middle Road, 311 lots) also lodged after being excluded from the Napier-Hastings Future Development Strategy

Continued expansion of the recurring-income commercial/industrial rental portfolio (Wairakei Road industrial development in Harewood, Christchurch, provides a mix of land sales and retained lots for lease), building on the 2019 diversification strategy

Opportunistic land acquisitions during down-cycles: management explicitly used subdued FY2025 conditions to acquire land in Havelock North (0.36ha) and Hamilton (1.76ha) to strengthen Fast-track applications, plus settled 6.5ha in Ruakura under an Overseas Investment Act consent
Regional diversification (Christchurch continuing to perform relatively well through the downturn) reduces dependence on any single metro market
Eventual cyclical recovery in NZ residential demand as mortgage rates ease and consenting/supply constraints bind, for which CDI is positioning inventory to be 'ready to meet demand'
New $20m ANZ credit facility (Aug-2026) provides additional dry powder to accelerate development or acquisitions without drawing down cash reserves further

business.description: FY2025 property sales fell to $34.5m (87 sections) from $46.0m (92 sections) in FY2024 as buyers 'sat on their hands' despite easing rates; management explicitly guided FY2026 earnings 'considerably lower' than FY2025 due to renewed geopolitical/economic uncertainty denting the early-2026 recovery signs.

Revenue is recognised only on settlement of titled sections; large developments (e.g., Prestons Park, just completed after 12 years) can concentrate hundreds of section sales in specific years, making period-to-period comparisons and short-term forecasting difficult.

46% of the 305ha landholding sits in a single growth cell (Ruakura 2, Hamilton) not yet consented; Hawke's Bay concentration (26%, Havelock North) is also material and has already seen one Fast-track application (Iona Stage 3) rejected at council level before being escalated via Fast-track referral.
Board explicitly discloses that 'institutional knowledge currently sits predominantly with the CEO' in a team that only grew from 5 to 8 employees in 2025.
Weather, contractor capacity, supply chain and consenting delays can push out section availability and sales timing, as already evidenced by multi-stage title delays at Iona.

financial.risk: Cash burn and now first-ever debt facility
financial.description: Cash fell from $32.8m to $13.4m in FY2025 (net operating outflow $9.0m plus $9.8m of dividends paid) as the company reinvests in growing its land bank; CDI entered a new NZ$20m credit facility with ANZ Bank around 7-Aug-2026 — the company's first debt facility in recent history, introducing balance-sheet leverage and interest-cost/covenant risk where none previously existed.

financial.risk: Interest rate sensitivity of investment income
financial.description: A 1 percentage point change in rates would move FY2025 pre-tax profit by only ~$0.12m given depleted cash balances (down from $0.47m sensitivity in FY2024) — a declining natural income buffer as cash is deployed into land.

Development and investment property are subject to independent valuer judgement (sales comparison / residual subdivision / income capitalisation approaches); a sustained downturn in section prices or investment property capitalisation-rate expansion could trigger impairment, though none was identified at FY2025.

regulatory.risk: Fast-track Approvals Act policy and appeal risk
regulatory.description: Fast-track consents (e.g., Arataki, subject to an appeal period) materially shorten timelines but remain a relatively new legislative mechanism; adverse court/appeal outcomes, changes to the Act, or a change of government policy could delay or derail the Ruakura 2 and other Fast-track-dependent pipeline.

Ongoing national/regional resource-management reform is forcing councils to reassess growth sequencing and land classifications, extending timeframes across the sector (explicitly flagged in the Chair's Review); Iona Stage 3 was excluded from the Napier-Hastings Future Development Strategy despite an independent hearing panel recommendation to approve it, forcing CDI onto the Fast-track referral pathway instead.

1-Apr-2024 removal of tax depreciation on commercial/industrial buildings created a one-off $3.9m deferred tax charge in FY2024, illustrating the rental portfolio's exposure to sudden central-government tax policy shifts.

macro.risk: Official Cash Rate and mortgage rate path
macro.description: RBNZ held OCR at 2.25% in Feb-2026 with market/ANZ pricing an increase from around Dec-2026; a faster-than-expected rate rise would weigh on already-fragile purchaser confidence and financing costs for both buyers and CDI's own construction funding.
NZ unemployment rose to 5.4% (Dec-2025, underutilisation 12.9%); management directly links job-security concerns to purchasers deferring section purchases.
Net migration gain fell to 14,200 in 2025 from 23,800 in 2024, reducing a key structural driver of housing demand.

macro.risk: House price stagnation / high existing-home inventory
macro.description: National median house price ($790,000 at 31-Dec-2025) remains 14.6% below the Nov-2021 peak; high existing-home inventory gives buyers lower-risk alternatives to new-build sections, competing directly with CDI's core product.
Elevated building costs are repeatedly cited by management as a factor causing purchasers to defer decisions, compressing achievable margins or slowing sell-down rates.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ residential land/housing market remains subdued in mid-2026: RBNZ holding OCR at 2.25% with a possible first hike from December 2026 (ANZ forecast); fixed mortgage rates broadly in the 4.5-5.0% range; building consents have begun trending up off a low base but remain well below the 2021 peak; forecasters see only modest (3-6%) house-price appreciation in 2026 given tight supply offset by weak demand.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — CDI operates in a classically cyclical, capital-intensive land-development industry where section sales volumes and prices move with interest rates, consumer confidence, employment and migration; company mitigates (does not eliminate) cyclicality via balance-sheet strength, regional diversification and a growing rental income leg.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high on the demand side (purchaser affordability/confidence) and low-to-moderate directly on CDI's own P&L (no debt historically, though the new $20m ANZ facility introduces incremental sensitivity; interest income on cash balances has shrunk as cash was deployed into land).

recent_developments.event: Fast-track application lodged for Arataki Road development, Havelock North (171 residential sections)

FY2025 result: profit after tax $11.1m (2024: $15.4m), revenue & other income $38.1m (2024: $49.1m), reflecting subdued residential market; shareholders' funds stable at $321.2m; total assets $331.6m; NTA 109.7 cps
Completed construction at Prestons Park, Christchurch — the company's flagship post-earthquake development, delivering >1,000 residential sections over its life since 2014
Julian Smith appointed independent director, restoring an independent Board majority after long-serving independent director John Henderson retired in May 2025

Fast-track Panel approved the Arataki Road consent (171 sections), expected to save roughly two years versus conventional RMA consenting; earthworks planned for the 2026/27 construction season, first sections expected end-2027

Board declared a fully imputed FY2025 final dividend of 1.0 cent per share (payable 15-May-2026, record date 1-May-2026), down from 3.5 cents per share paid in respect of FY2024; Dividend Reinvestment Plan applies
FY2025 Annual Report published; Board flagged 'cautiously optimistic' outlook for FY2026 but noted any recovery in residential demand would be gradual

April 2026 YTD trading update (per AGM deck): residential section settlements of $5.7m, unconditional sales yet to settle of $10.6m, conditional sales yet to confirm/settle of $2.5m; management noted these sales were 'secured before the market turned'

42nd Annual Meeting of Shareholders: all three resolutions passed (re-election of Eik Sheng Kwek, election of Julian Smith, auditor remuneration), each with >99% support; management explicitly guided that 'earnings for 2026 [are expected to be] considerably lower than those reported in 2025' due to renewed geopolitical uncertainty eroding early-2026 signs of recovery

CDL Investments New Zealand entered a new NZ$20 million flexible credit facility with ANZ Bank — the company's first meaningful debt facility (balance sheet was debt-free at FY2025 year-end), likely intended to support development funding/liquidity as cash reserves have been drawn down and Fast-track projects move toward capital-intensive construction phases

items.notes: Both the Chair's AGM remarks and the CEO's outlook slide state explicitly that FY2026 earnings are expected to be 'considerably lower' than FY2025 given renewed geopolitical uncertainty that has stalled the early-2026 signs of residential recovery; no specific numeric range was provided.

items.target: Secure section sales and investment property revenue for another profitable year; continue disciplined capital allocation; advance Fast-track projects (Ruakura 2 lodgement targeted by end-2026); maintain balance sheet flexibility for opportunistic acquisitions
items.vs_prior: maintained (consistent strategic framework, no quantitative KPI issued)
items.notes: No formal revenue, margin or unit-sales guidance range is issued by CDI; management guidance is qualitative/directional only, consistent with prior years.

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Desleigh Jameson (AGM, 26-May-2026): 'Given the current economic climate and prevailing geopolitical uncertainties, we expect earnings for 2026 to be considerably lower than those reported in 2025... CDI enters this period from a position of strength... a robust balance sheet... sufficient flexibility to adapt as conditions evolve and to capitalise when the economy improves.' CEO Jason Adams (AGM outlook slide): 'The encouraging signs of a residential recovery we saw at the beginning of the year, have not continued. Recent geopolitics has impacted confidence and slowed the momentum that started to emerge... Our focus remains on securing sales, preserving cash flow and continuing to plan for our future.'

bull_case: Debt-free (until the small new $20m facility), cash-generative-through-cycle balance sheet backed by a well-capitalised Singapore-linked parent (Hong Leong/CDL) lets CDI outlast smaller, leveraged competitors in a residential downturn and buy land opportunistically when others are forced sellers, as it did in FY2025 (Havelock North and Hamilton acquisitions)

Land bank materially undervalued on the balance sheet relative to independent market valuations ($339.3m residential + $68.9m commercial valuations vs lower carrying costs), providing a margin-of-safety and future profit-recognition runway as sections settle

Multi-year Fast-track pipeline (Arataki Road approved; Ruakura 2's ~1,350 lots and 35ha commercial land to be lodged by end-2026) materially expands consented/near-consented inventory ahead of the next up-cycle, with Fast-track saving roughly two years of RMA process time versus peers still in conventional consenting queues
Growing, high-occupancy recurring rental income (near-100% occupied industrial warehouses, 4.0-year WALE) diversifies earnings and reduces pure dependence on residential-sale timing

NZ residential cycle is a well-understood, historically mean-reverting market; falling OCR/mortgage rates (though not yet enough to unlock demand) set up a plausible multi-year recovery tailwind once confidence and employment stabilise, with CDI positioned with 'ready' inventory to capture it
bear_case: Management has explicitly guided FY2026 earnings 'considerably lower' than FY2025's already-reduced $11.1m, with no numeric floor given — visibility is poor and consensus/investor expectations could still be too high

Revenue is structurally lumpy and settlement-timed; a soft, uncertain macro backdrop (unemployment rising to 5.4%, net migration nearly halving, geopolitical shocks reportedly re-stalling a nascent 2026 recovery) could push settlements out further, compounding cash-flow pressure

Cash reserves nearly halved in FY2025 ($32.8m to $13.4m) and the company has now taken on its first debt facility (NZ$20m ANZ, Aug-2026), eroding the pristine, debt-free balance sheet that has been its central competitive claim and introducing new interest-cost/covenant risk into a still-cyclical business

65.12% majority control by Millennium & Copthorne Hotels NZ (ultimately Hong Leong/CDL Singapore) leaves minority shareholders reliant on a related-party-heavy governance structure for capital-allocation, dividend and any future privatisation/takeover decisions; the free float is thin (only 35% non-MCK, with a further 8.14% held by a single individual, Adrian Ho, meaning roughly three-quarters of the register sits with two holders) and liquidity is limited

Regulatory/consenting risk is real even under Fast-track: Iona Stage 3 was excluded from the formal Napier-Hastings Future Development Strategy despite an independent panel recommendation to approve it, showing that even well-advanced CDI projects can be rejected by elected councils and require fallback routes; broader RMA/planning-reform transition is adding complexity and extending timeframes sector-wide
management_commentary_summary: At the 26-May-2026 AGM, Chair Desleigh Jameson characterised 2025 as a 'challenging year' in which easing mortgage rates were not enough to restore purchaser confidence given cost-of-living pressures, building costs, employment uncertainty and broader economic pressure. She reiterated CDI's core discipline (protect value, preserve balance-sheet strength, keep the pipeline moving) and highlighted the Arataki Road Fast-track consent (saving roughly two years of RMA process) as a key achievement, alongside continuing work on Fast-track applications in Hamilton (Ruakura 2) and Havelock North (Iona Stage 3), both expected to be lodged before end-2026. She explicitly guided that FY2026 earnings are expected to be 'considerably lower' than FY2025 given the current economic climate and geopolitical uncertainty, but stressed CDI enters the period 'from a position of strength' with a robust balance sheet and flexibility to capitalise when conditions improve. CEO Jason Adams's operational update reinforced this: encouraging early-2026 signs of a residential recovery 'have not continued,' with recent geopolitical developments dampening confidence; management's stated priorities for 2026 are securing sales, preserving cash flow, and continuing to plan/consent the pipeline (including advancing the Ruakura 2 and Iona Fast-track lodgements) so CDI is positioned to benefit when the cycle turns, noting April 2026 YTD settlements of $5.7m plus a further $13.1m of unconditional/conditional sales yet to settle, which management said were 'fortunate' to have been secured 'before the market turned.'
dividend_policy: CDI has historically paid an annual (sometimes semi-annual) fully imputed ordinary dividend funded from profits, reflecting a policy of balancing shareholder returns against retaining capital for development, Fast-track project funding and potential land acquisitions. The FY2024 dividend was 3.5 cents per share (paid 2025); the Board reduced this materially to 1.0 cent per share fully imputed for FY2025 (declared 24-Feb-2026, paid 15-May-2026, record date 1-May-2026), consistent with the lower FY2025 profit and a more cautious capital-retention stance heading into an expected weaker FY2026. CDI operates a Dividend Reinvestment Plan (DRP), in place since 1998, under which shareholders can elect to receive dividends as cash or as additional shares issued at the weighted-average market price over the first five business days following the record date; the DRP applied to both the FY2024 dividend (1,038,719 new shares issued at $0.6961) and the FY2025 final dividend, and management has indicated part of the FY2025 dividend will again be satisfied via DRP shares, providing CDI a partial non-dilutive-to-cash mechanism to retain capital while still rewarding shareholders. The company also pays a supplementary dividend to non-resident shareholders to offset non-resident withholding tax, recovered via a foreign investor tax credit.

ownership.majority_shareholder: Millennium & Copthorne Hotels New Zealand Limited (NZX:MCK) — 190,591,297 shares, 65.12% of issued capital as at 27-Feb-2026 (65.31% at FY2024 year-end)
ownership.ultimate_parent_chain: MCK is 83.84% owned (on voting shares) by CDL Hotels Holdings New Zealand Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of London-domiciled Millennium & Copthorne Hotels Limited; the ultimate holding company is Hong Leong Investment Holdings Pte Ltd, Singapore (the Kwek family's Hong Leong Group, which also controls Singapore-listed City Developments Limited, CDL). MCK has one of CDI's five Board seats (Non-Executive Director Vincent Yeo; fellow Hong Leong/CDL group executive Eik Sheng Kwek also sits on the Board as a Non-Executive Director representing the wider group).
ownership.second_largest_holder: Adrian Ho — 23,832,598 shares, 8.14% of issued capital (a substantial product holder alongside MCK per FMCA notices)
ownership.free_float: Approximately 27% of issued capital is genuinely free-floating once MCK (65.12%) and Adrian Ho (8.14%) are excluded; institutional/custodial holders (ACC-NZCSD 4.53%, Citibank Nominees 2.06%, NZX WT Nominees 1.22%) hold most of the remainder. 2,376 total shareholders on the register; the top 13 holders (each owning >1,000,000 shares) control 85.27% of shares on issue. 87.1% of shareholders (by number) and shares are NZ-domiciled; 12.9% are Australian/overseas holders.
ownership.implications: Majority control by MCK/Hong Leong effectively removes CDI from ordinary takeover risk (no third party can gain control without MCK's consent) and provides implicit parental financial support/expertise, but it also means minority shareholders have limited influence over strategy, capital allocation, board composition, and dividend policy — governance relies on the independent-director majority (currently 3 of 5: Jameson, Elrick, Smith) and the Audit & Risk Committee (chaired by an independent director) rather than shareholder votes to protect minority interests. Related-party transactions with MCK (shared office costs, insurance, recharges — $596,787 in FY2025) are modest but recurring. The thin free float (~27%) and concentrated top-holder base likely constrain secondary-market liquidity and could contribute to a persistent valuation discount or wide bid-ask spreads; no directors hold any shares personally (per FY2025 statutory disclosures), somewhat limiting direct insider alignment with the minority shareholder base beyond the parent's economic interest.
